A signed message can be copied and presented again. Its signature proves that specific bytes were signed; it does not, by itself, prove that the permission is still active or unused.
Replay protection depends on the consumer checking the authorization’s scope, time window, and use state.
Authorization nonce: part of a principal-signed permission. PriorSeal also carries a maxUses limit; the usual single-use setting is 1.
EVM transaction nonce: part of a sender’s transaction sequence on a specific chain. It helps correlate an observed transaction, but it is not the authorization’s use counter.
External decision reference: a digest can bind an external decision to an authorization. That binding does not automatically make the external decision single-use across multiple authorizations.

Hi everyone!
A fast, free, and simple online video compressor with no watermarks or limits on use.
The Problem
You've got a ton of free online video compressors to choose from, though most of those services will throw a lot of frustrating restrictions on you watermarks, file size limits, and hidden paywalls.
The Tech Stack
The project is developed with:
Frontend: Next JS, static site generation and an ultra-fast UI.

This allowed me to shift the compression to the server side so that I could take advantage of full CPU and I/O performance of the machine.

Optimize compression presets dynamically
Manage bigger uploads
Compatibility to various video formats, like MP4, MOV, AVI, etc.
Lessons Learned
Sure, frontend compression sounds neat and all, but when you got some serious grind to do, ain't worth the effort.

It's totally free, no watermarks, no hidden limits.
Would appreciate your comments or suggestions of improvement!

articles.author: probeo
articles.description:
I look after a small handheld oscilloscope here in the UK. It's the one I pick up for quick checks when setting up a bench scope isn't worth it. These are my notes on using it.
The BSIDE OT3: a 10 MHz handheld digital oscilloscope with a 3.2" TFT screen and 48 MSa/s sampling, on one analogue channel. It runs on a built-in 3.7 V 1200 mAh battery and charges over USB Type-C.
Long-press the power key to turn it on.
Connect the BNC probe or the alligator-clip lead to the right-hand input.
Clip ground to the circuit's ground, then put the probe tip on the signal.
Press AUTO to scale the waveform.
Use the direction keys to adjust timebase and volts per division by hand if AUTO isn't quite right.
Slower signals sit comfortably inside 10 MHz: audio paths, PWM, and on cars things like injectors and crank or cam sensors. It isn't a 50 or 100 MHz bench scope, and fast digital edges above its rating won't look right, so I don't use it for those.
Holding start/pause saves a screen image. The images come off over USB Type-C, and firmware updates use the same port.
The menus are in Chinese and English.
The probe uses a standard BNC connector, so a longer lead can be swapped in.
It goes back on charge after a day of use rather than being left flat in the drawer.
The scope I'm describing is the one on probeo.co.uk.
articles.title: How I use a 10 MHz handheld oscilloscope for quick checks
